questions.prompt: What is plasma?
options: The liquid part of blood, containing water and dissolved substances.
The nucleus of a red cell.
The wall of every artery.
A gas inside a red cell.
questions.explanation: Plasma suspends formed elements and carries dissolved materials. It is mostly water, but also contains proteins, ions and other substances.

questions.prompt: Which is a cell fragment rather than a complete cell?
options: A neutrophil.
A platelet.
A lymphocyte.
An endothelial cell.
questions.explanation: Platelets are fragments released by large bone-marrow cells. They help form a plug at vessel damage.

questions.prompt: Which human blood component normally has a nucleus?
options: A mature red blood cell.
Plasma.
A white blood cell.
A platelet fragment.
questions.explanation: White cells are complete nucleated cells. Mature human red cells lack a nucleus, and platelets are fragments.

questions.prompt: Which component normally occupies the largest fraction of whole-blood volume in the teaching example?
options: White cells alone.
Platelets alone.
Dissolved oxygen alone.
Plasma.
questions.explanation: The example has 55% plasma by volume, a very thin buffy coat and about 45% red cells. These are illustrative values, not fixed for every person.

questions.prompt: In an anticoagulated sample after centrifugation, which layer is at the bottom?
options: The packed red-cell layer.
A layer of pure oxygen.
A layer of antibodies only.
A layer of the least-dense plasma.
questions.explanation: The denser red cells collect below plasma and the thin buffy coat. Separation is physical, not production of new blood components.

questions.prompt: What is in the buffy coat?
options: Only haemoglobin molecules.
White cells and platelets.
Only pure water.
Only oxygenated red cells.
questions.explanation: The buffy coat is a thin pale layer containing white cells and platelets between plasma and packed red cells.

questions.prompt: What do the heights of separated blood layers mainly represent?
options: The number of oxygen molecules in each layer.
The percentage of cells with a nucleus.
Fractions of blood volume.
The speed of blood in an artery.
questions.explanation: Layer heights in a uniform tube indicate approximate volume fractions. They do not directly count cells.

questions.prompt: Why does the centrifuge sample contain an anticoagulant?
options: To turn plasma into red cells.
To make all cells the same density.
To give the red cells oxygen bubbles.
To prevent clotting while components are separated.
questions.explanation: An anticoagulant prevents coagulation, allowing plasma and formed elements to be separated. A clotting sample instead leaves serum around a clot.

questions.prompt: A tube contains 55% plasma and 0.5% buffy coat by volume. What fraction remains for red cells?
questions.explanation: The fractions must total 100%: 100 − 55 − 0.5 = 44.5%. This example illustrates volume, not cell-number percentages.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes plasma and serum?
options: Plasma is a gas but serum is a liquid.
Serum is the liquid remaining after blood clots and lacks fibrinogen consumed in clotting.
Serum contains all the red cells and plasma contains none.
They always contain exactly the same clotting proteins.
questions.explanation: Plasma from anticoagulated blood retains clotting proteins. During clotting, fibrinogen is converted into fibrin, so the remaining serum differs.

questions.prompt: What carries most oxygen in human blood?
options: Platelet nuclei.
Air bubbles in plasma.
Haemoglobin inside red blood cells.
Urea dissolved in plasma.
questions.explanation: Oxygen binds reversibly to haemoglobin. A small amount is dissolved, but most is carried by red cells.

questions.prompt: What does biconcave mean for a red cell?
options: It has two nuclei.
It has two separate chambers.
It contains two air bubbles.
It has an inward dip on each face.
questions.explanation: A biconcave disc is thinner centrally on both faces. This supports a large exchange surface relative to volume and a short diffusion distance.

questions.prompt: How does flexibility help a red cell?
options: It can deform through narrow capillaries.
It can make a new nucleus in every vessel.
It can turn into a vein valve.
It can pump blood without the heart.
questions.explanation: Red cells often pass through capillaries in single file and deform without normally leaving the intact vessel.

questions.prompt: What colour is normal oxygen-poor blood?
options: Blue.
Dark red.
Colourless.
Green.
questions.explanation: Blood remains red because of haemoglobin. Diagrams sometimes colour return routes blue or purple, but this is a drawing convention.

questions.prompt: Where does oxygen normally load onto haemoglobin?
options: Inside the kidney collecting duct.
Only inside a platelet plug.
In blood passing the lung exchange surface.
In a vein valve pocket that makes oxygen.
questions.explanation: At the lungs, oxygen diffuses from alveolar air into blood and binds haemoglobin. It can unload at body tissues.

questions.prompt: What normally happens to a red cell when it supplies oxygen to muscle?
options: It bursts into the muscle to release an air bubble.
It becomes a muscle cell permanently.
It changes into an antibody.
It remains inside the vessel while oxygen transfers towards tissue.
questions.explanation: Oxygen unloads and diffuses across the exchange surface; whole red cells normally remain in intact vessels.

questions.prompt: Why is lacking a nucleus useful for a mature human red cell?
options: It leaves more room for haemoglobin.
It allows the cell to produce antibodies.
It makes it a larger white cell.
It makes blood pressure disappear.
questions.explanation: Loss of the nucleus supports the red cell’s specialised carrying role. It also limits its ability to make repairs and new proteins.

questions.prompt: A muscle uses oxygen rapidly during exercise. What helps oxygen move from blood towards the muscle?
options: The muscle making blood blue.
A maintained difference in oxygen partial pressure.
All capillary walls becoming thick muscle.
Platelets converting glucose into oxygen.
questions.explanation: Oxygen use helps maintain a gradient. Blood flow brings more oxygen, and oxygen can unload from haemoglobin and diffuse towards tissue.

questions.prompt: If haemoglobin is reduced while plasma volume stays similar, what direct transport function may be reduced?
options: The direction defining an artery.
The conversion of every vein into a capillary.
The capacity to carry oxygen bound to haemoglobin.
The number of air bubbles held in blood.
questions.explanation: Less haemoglobin can reduce oxygen-carrying capacity. This model does not diagnose a cause or predict an individual’s symptoms.

questions.prompt: Which comparison best connects structure and function?
options: A thick rigid cube is needed to pass in single file.
A large nucleus is the main oxygen-binding structure.
A platelet’s fragments carry more oxygen because they are smaller.
A dipped flexible disc supports gas exchange and passage through narrow vessels.
questions.explanation: A biconcave red cell has a favourable surface-to-volume relationship, short diffusion distances and flexibility; haemoglobin binds the oxygen.

questions.prompt: How does most glucose travel through the blood?
options: Dissolved in plasma.
As bubbles in the heart.
As the nucleus of a platelet.
Only bound to oxygen in red cells.
questions.explanation: Glucose is carried in the liquid plasma. Entering many body cells then requires appropriate membrane transport proteins.

questions.prompt: Which journey correctly describes urea?
options: Lungs to red cells, then release as oxygen.
Liver to kidneys in plasma, then excretion in urine.
Platelets to arteries, then conversion into glucose.
Kidneys to lungs, then excretion as the main breathed gas.
questions.explanation: The liver makes urea while processing excess nitrogen from amino acids. Blood carries it to the kidneys for excretion.

questions.prompt: What is a hormone?
options: A new type of blood vessel wall.
An oxygen bubble trapped in a platelet.
A chemical signal that can travel to target cells.
An organ that filters every red cell.
questions.explanation: Endocrine glands release hormones into blood. A responding cell needs the appropriate receptor and cell machinery.

questions.prompt: What is an ion in plasma?
options: A whole artery.
A large group of white cells only.
A bubble of air.
An electrically charged particle.
questions.explanation: Ions such as sodium, chloride and bicarbonate are charged particles dissolved in the watery plasma.

questions.prompt: How is most carbon dioxide transported in blood?
options: As bicarbonate ions in plasma, formed largely through reactions in red cells.
As large air bubbles in arteries.
Only as carbon dioxide in platelet nuclei.
Only as solid carbon particles.
questions.explanation: Most transported CO₂ is converted to bicarbonate. Some also remains dissolved or binds haemoglobin, so the plasma route is not the only route.

questions.prompt: Why does a circulating hormone not make every cell respond in the same way?
options: Hormones never leave the heart.
Response depends on appropriate receptors and internal machinery.
Only red cells receive any blood flow.
All tissues have identical responses to every signal.
questions.explanation: Blood distributes a hormone widely, but recognition and response are selective. Many hormones also travel bound to plasma proteins.

questions.prompt: Which is a function of albumin in plasma?
options: Binding most oxygen in place of haemoglobin.
Making every white cell lose its nucleus.
Helping retain water in circulation and carrying some substances.
Acting as a one-way vein valve.
questions.explanation: Albumin contributes to plasma’s osmotic effects and can bind some cargo, including fatty acids and some hormones.

questions.prompt: What is redistributed when warm blood flows from working muscle towards skin?
options: A special molecule made only of heat.
New oxygen atoms made by the skin.
Cold red cells that cancel temperature.
Thermal energy.
questions.explanation: Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference. Circulating blood, including its water-rich plasma, redistributes thermal energy.

questions.prompt: Why would removing only red cells not remove all transported carbon-dioxide equivalents?
options: Much is present as bicarbonate dissolved in plasma.
All carbon dioxide is attached to platelet membranes.
Carbon dioxide can travel only in empty vessels.
Red cells never take part in carbon-dioxide chemistry.
questions.explanation: Red cells help convert CO₂ into bicarbonate, but much bicarbonate then travels in plasma. Production location and travelling medium need not be identical.

questions.prompt: Why must a blood transport map not show a direct liver-to-kidney shortcut as the whole journey?
options: The liver and kidneys never receive any blood.
Blood normally passes through the returning circulation, right heart, lungs and left heart between systemic organs.
Urea has to travel only through the trachea.
Kidneys receive blood only from platelet plugs.
questions.explanation: The simplified sequence connects organ functions, not a single direct vessel. Route diagrams should preserve the two-circuit circulation.

questions.prompt: Which component includes cells that can engulf microbes?
options: Red blood cells only.
Glucose.
White blood cells.
Urea.
questions.explanation: Neutrophils and some other immune cells can engulf material. White cells have varied roles and do not all perform every immune task.

questions.prompt: What are antibodies?
options: Tiny arteries.
Red cells filled with air.
The same thing as platelets.
Proteins that recognise particular molecular targets.
questions.explanation: Some lymphocytes develop into antibody-producing cells. Antibodies are dissolved proteins, not miniature white cells.

questions.prompt: What do platelets first help form at a damaged vessel?
options: A local plug.
A new lung.
A bubble carrying oxygen.
A layer of pure glucose.
questions.explanation: Platelets adhere and aggregate at damaged surfaces. Other vessel and clotting responses contribute to stopping bleeding.

questions.prompt: What forms the stabilising strands in a clot?
options: Glucose.
Fibrin.
Oxygen gas.
Urea.
questions.explanation: Clotting reactions convert soluble fibrinogen from plasma into insoluble fibrin strands, which help stabilise a platelet plug.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly compares white cells?
options: Every white cell carries most blood oxygen.
Every white cell is a nucleus-free fragment.
Different types have different immune roles.
All white cells make identical antibodies all the time.
questions.explanation: The family includes several cell types. Neutrophils can engulf microbes; lymphocytes perform a variety of specific immune roles.

questions.prompt: How can some white cells reach affected tissue?
options: All white cells burst through any artery wall at random.
They always change into red cells before leaving.
They never act outside the heart.
They can leave suitable small vessels through controlled processes.
questions.explanation: Immune cells can move across appropriate vessel walls and through tissues. This is different from red cells normally remaining inside intact vessels.

questions.prompt: Why are both platelets and plasma important in clotting?
options: Platelets make a plug and plasma provides proteins for the fibrin mesh.
Platelets are simply solid plasma with no special role.
Plasma contains no clotting proteins.
Only red cells can make any repair.
questions.explanation: A plug is strengthened by the coagulation system. Fibrinogen and other clotting proteins circulate in plasma before local activation.

questions.prompt: A healing wound needs oxygen as well as a plug. Which components best match these two jobs?
options: Platelets for most oxygen; glucose for the plug.
Red cells for most oxygen transport; platelets for the plug.
Urea for oxygen; vein valves for the plug.
White cells for every job and no other components.
questions.explanation: The location alone does not choose the component. Different cargos and repair stages require different blood components.

questions.prompt: Why can a clot inside an undamaged vessel be harmful?
options: It always increases oxygen delivery to all tissues.
It turns blood into pure water.
It can obstruct blood flow and reduce downstream supply.
It creates a new correct circulation route.
questions.explanation: Clotting is useful at a break but an obstruction in the circulation can interrupt transport. The teaching model does not simulate clinical treatment.

questions.prompt: Which statement avoids a common immunity mix-up?
options: All white cells are identical antibody containers.
Antibodies are small red cells.
Platelets are the only cells that recognise every microbe.
Some lymphocytes give rise to antibody-producing cells; neutrophils have other important roles.
questions.explanation: White-cell diversity matters. Antibodies are proteins produced by specialised cells, while other white cells have different defensive actions.

questions.prompt: What defines an artery?
options: Carrying blood away from the heart.
Always carrying oxygen-rich blood.
Having the lowest pressure in the body.
Always containing pocket valves.
questions.explanation: Direction defines the vessel type. The pulmonary artery is an important oxygen-poor example.

questions.prompt: What defines a vein?
options: Always carrying blue blood.
Returning blood towards the heart.
Always having a one-cell-thick wall only.
Making oxygen inside its lumen.
questions.explanation: Veins return blood to the heart. The pulmonary veins carry oxygen-rich blood; all normal blood remains red.

questions.prompt: What is the lumen?
options: The entire surrounding muscle.
A white cell’s nucleus.
The space inside a vessel.
The iron inside haemoglobin.
questions.explanation: Blood flows along the lumen. Wall thickness and lumen size are separate structural features.

questions.prompt: Which wall is best suited to short-distance exchange?
options: An extremely thick multilayer artery wall.
A thick bone wall.
A closed vein valve.
A thin capillary wall.
questions.explanation: A thin endothelial layer and supporting layer shorten the distance for exchange. Different capillary types have different permeability.

questions.prompt: Why do arteries have substantial elastic and muscular layers?
options: To withstand and respond to higher pulsatile pressure.
To make blood blue.
To stop every red cell permanently.
To filter out all glucose before it reaches tissues.
questions.explanation: Elastic tissue can stretch and recoil; smooth muscle helps regulate vessel diameter. Structure suits the pressure and distribution role.

questions.prompt: What do pocket valves in many limb veins do?
options: Create new oxygen molecules.
Limit reverse flow when pressure would drive blood backwards.
Make the vein into an artery.
Pump blood without any pressure difference.
questions.explanation: Leaflets close against backflow and open with forward flow. They do not generate the pressure difference themselves.

questions.prompt: Why should a capillary not be shown with thick layers of muscle?
options: All blood vessels are solid muscle rods.
A capillary contains no living cells at all.
Its exchange wall is a thin endothelial layer with a thin supporting layer.
Thick muscle is required for every gas to diffuse.
questions.explanation: Capillaries specialise in exchange, whereas larger arteries and veins have more substantial layered walls.

questions.prompt: Which vessel can carry oxygen-poor blood away from the heart?
options: A pulmonary vein.
The aorta under normal conditions.
The left ventricle’s oxygen-rich systemic outflow only.
The pulmonary artery.
questions.explanation: The pulmonary artery takes blood from the right heart towards the lungs. Artery refers to direction, not oxygen content.

questions.prompt: A diagram colours return branches purple. What should the caption explain?
options: The colour identifies a route; real oxygen-poor blood is dark red.
The drawing proves veins contain purple plasma.
Red cells become blue when they lose oxygen.
Blood changes into ink before entering a vein.
questions.explanation: Colour coding is a visual convention. Haemoglobin-containing blood is red at both higher and lower oxygen saturation.

questions.prompt: Why is average blood speed lower across the overall capillary network than in the aorta?
options: Each capillary has a larger individual lumen than the aorta.
The network has a much larger total cross-sectional area.
Capillaries have a second heart pumping backwards.
Red cells stop moving permanently in every capillary.
questions.explanation: Continuity relates total flow to total area. Many narrow capillaries in parallel provide a very large combined area; this does not mean each is wider than the aorta.

questions.prompt: What does diffusion describe?
options: Every particle moving only one way with no randomness.
The heart physically pushing whole cells through all walls.
Net movement down a gradient due to random particle motion.
A process that always needs a platelet nucleus.
questions.explanation: Particles move randomly both ways; a gradient can produce a net transfer from higher to lower concentration or partial pressure.

questions.prompt: What is a gradient?
options: A type of white cell.
A valve found only in the aorta.
A bubble of plasma.
A difference across a distance.
questions.explanation: A concentration or partial-pressure difference across an exchange surface helps determine the direction of net diffusion.

questions.prompt: At body tissues using oxygen, which gas directions are expected?
options: Oxygen towards tissue and carbon dioxide towards blood.
Both gases only towards tissue in every situation.
Whole red cells out and no gases in.
Oxygen into blood from muscle and no carbon dioxide transfer.
questions.explanation: Tissue use of oxygen and production of carbon dioxide help maintain their separate gradients. Each gas has its own direction of net transfer.

questions.prompt: At the lungs, which direction normally applies to oxygen?
options: From plasma into a platelet nucleus only.
From alveolar air into blood.
From the kidneys into the trachea directly.
From red cells to a vein valve that makes air.
questions.explanation: Ventilation renews alveolar air and circulation renews blood, maintaining the conditions for oxygen loading and carbon-dioxide removal.

questions.prompt: Why does a thinner exchange barrier help diffusion?
options: It creates new oxygen from nothing.
It forces all blood cells to leave vessels.
It shortens the distance particles cross.
It makes the whole circulation stop.
questions.explanation: Other conditions being comparable, a short path helps exchange. Surface area, gradients and permeability also matter.

questions.prompt: What should happen to most large plasma proteins at a typical intact exchange surface?
options: They all pass as freely as oxygen in every capillary.
They all become air bubbles.
They all turn into red cells at every heartbeat.
They mainly remain in the circulation.
questions.explanation: Permeability depends on the vessel type and substance. A capillary is not an open gap that releases every blood component.

questions.prompt: Which change is the fairest way to compare gas-exchange direction in the lab?
options: Switch between body and lung capillaries while keeping the vessel view comparable.
Change every setting and assume one change caused everything.
Compare an artery wall with an unrelated plasma volume percentage only.
Use the number of purple route lines as an oxygen measurement.
questions.explanation: Changing the location tests the direction associated with that exchange surface. The qualitative model does not produce clinical transfer rates.

questions.prompt: What does O₂ mean?
options: Two entire red cells.
One molecule containing two oxygen atoms.
An oxygen pressure of exactly two pascals.
A second type of platelet.
questions.explanation: The subscript counts atoms in the molecule. CO₂ instead has one carbon and two oxygen atoms; these formulas do not name blood components.

questions.prompt: Why must visible cells in this simulation not be counted to estimate a real white-cell fraction?
options: Real blood contains equal counts of all components.
A white-cell count equals the number of map branches.
Rare components are deliberately enlarged and overrepresented for inspection.
All colours are actual percentages.
questions.explanation: The model is qualitative. A laboratory count or a calibrated measurement is needed for quantitative proportions; illustrative cell placement is not data.

questions.prompt: Which interpretation separates flow from exchange?
options: Flow means all cells crossing the wall into tissue.
Exchange means the heart changing into a lung.
Flow and diffusion are identical mechanisms.
Blood flow brings material to a region; exchange transfers substances across appropriate barriers.
questions.explanation: Bulk circulation moves blood along vessels. Diffusion and other suitable transport routes then move substances across exchange surfaces and cell membranes.
